book.tiangongkaiwu.naili.name: Tiangong Kaiwu: On Grains (Naili)
book.tiangongkaiwu.naili.tooltip: Translate fragments at the Hanmo Tai to continue the unfinished text of this scroll.
book.tiangongkaiwu.naili.description: Naili comes first: the five grains are the very lifeblood of the people. From the General Discourse onward, entries on rice, wheat, millet, hemp and beans — and on rice lands, rice work, rice calamities and water works — unfold one by one. Translate fragments at the Hanmo Tai to continue the unfinished text of this scroll.
category.tiangongkaiwu.naili_juan.name: On Grains (Naili)
category.tiangongkaiwu.naili_juan.descri: The five grains are the lifeblood of the people.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_zonglun.name: General Discourse
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_zonglun.page1: Master Song says: Shennong of high antiquity hovers between being and nothingness, yet the two words of his title have endured to this day. Man cannot prolong his own life, yet the five grains prolong it for him; the five grains cannot sow themselves, yet men sow them.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_do.name: Rice
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_do.page1: Rice comes in more varieties than any other grain, and the first thing to learn about a variety is stickiness. The non-glutinous plant is called jing; its husked grain, jingmi, cooks into firm, dry rice. The glutinous plant is called tu; its grain, nuomi, is sticky and made into wine and cakes. In the south no sticky millet is grown, so nearly all wine is brewed from glutinous rice.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_do.page2: Even within one kind the grain differs: awns long or short, kernels round or pointed, and names that change with local custom. Early and late varieties ripen weeks apart, so the farmer sows them in turn and keeps his fields green through the seasons.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_do.page3: Once the rice is in the field, the real work begins: which soil suits it, how it must be ploughed and harrowed, how flood, drought and insects are kept at bay, and how water is brought to it. These four matters are the subjects of the entries that follow — rice lands, rice work, rice calamities and water works.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_mai.name: Wheat
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_mai.page1: Wheat has fewer names than rice, but they are drawn clearly. Common wheat is called lai, chief of the wheats; barley is called mou, and also kuang. The oat and the buckwheat are the lesser kinds.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_mai.page2: Buckwheat loves cool weather and is sown in late summer and early autumn. Its stems redden, its seed is three-cornered, and it grinds into flour for noodles and cakes; when the land is worn and famine threatens, it is the easiest crop to bring in.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_mai.page3: Wheat likes high, dry ground and cannot abide standing water. Winter wheat must be sown before the first hard frost and is reaped in early summer. Then beans or millet take its place in the same field, year following year, so the land is never worn out — wheat and beans in turn, a practice as old as farming itself.
